core: Layout as the arrangement of content on a page or screen so it reads as organized and scannable
The four C.R.A.P. layout/design principles — Contrast, Repetition, Alignment, Proximity — attributed to Robin Williams (The Non-Designer's Design Book)
Alignment in depth: edge (left/right/top/bottom) and center alignment, the shared invisible line, choosing one strong alignment
Proximity in depth: grouping related items, separating unrelated groups, forming visual units (Gestalt proximity)
White space (negative space) as an active layout tool: macro and micro, grouping, focus, readability
Reading flow and common scanning patterns (F-pattern, Z/Gutenberg), and designing with the reader's path
Print vs screen layout considerations (fixed page and margins vs responsive reflow)

Visual hierarchy as the outcome layout supports (owned by Visual Hierarchy topic)
Gestalt principle of proximity as the perceptual basis for grouping

claims.claim: The four widely-taught layout/design principles known as C.R.A.P. — Contrast, Repetition, Alignment, and Proximity — were laid out by Robin Williams in The Non-Designer's Design Book, a text used even in graphic-design programs.
Proximity means arranging items so that related items are grouped close together and unrelated items are separated, which establishes and signals relationships between elements.

Alignment means arranging items so that they touch common imaginary (invisible) vertical or horizontal lines, which conveys organization and a polished, deliberate look; choosing one strong alignment is generally stronger than mixing several.
White space (negative space) is an active layout tool rather than wasted space; it exists at macro and micro scales and supports grouping (proximity), focus, balance, and readability.

Readers of web pages tend to scan in an F-shaped pattern, with fixations concentrated at the top and along the left; this is a default tendency for unformatted text, not a law, and it is broken up by headings, bold text, lists, and images.
Grouping via proximity, whitespace, and enclosure, plus alignment, produces organized, scannable layouts that guide the eye to elements in an intended order (supporting visual hierarchy).

The C.R.A.P. principles are useful guidelines for readable, attractive documents in both print and on screen, but print layouts have fixed page dimensions and margins while screen layouts commonly reflow responsively across device sizes.
Emphasis and hierarchy are created by varying elements (size, visual intensity, colour, placement, and relationship to other elements); if everything is given equal weight, nothing stands out.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How firmly the F-pattern should be presented
positions: Popular design writing treats the F-pattern as a fixed law of how people read screens
Nielsen Norman Group frames it as a default tendency that appears with poorly-formatted text and is disrupted by good formatting
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a common default tendency and a reason to add structure (headings, lists, grouping), not as an inviolable rule, following NN/g.

sourceRecords.title: 3.1 C.R.A.P. Principles of Graphic Design (Business Information Systems: Design an App for That)
sourceRecords.notes: Open textbook section defining C.R.A.P. and crediting Robin Williams' The Non-Designer's Design Book as the source of the four 'survivor principles.' Supports: Contrast = using type/color/weight to draw attention; Repetition = repeating fonts/colors/images to unify a composition; Alignment = arranging items to touch common imaginary vertical/horizontal lines to convey organization; Proximity = grouping similar items to establish relationship; and that CRAP applies to both screen and print. Text was adapted by Saylor under CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 'without attribution as requested by the work's original creator'. Read via the saylordotorg.github.io copy on 2026-08-19. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Four Principles of Document Design (Howdy or Hello? Technical and Professional Communication)
sourceRecords.notes: OER chapter applying Robin Williams' four principles (contrast, repetition, alignment, proximity) to document design, naming The Non-Designer's Design Book as an essential reference used in design programs. Supports the invisible-line framing of alignment and the 'place related objects close together to show connectedness' framing of proximity, with print/document examples (resumes, captions near photos). Book license CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (page footer confirmed via curl; the plain fetcher received HTTP 403). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Non-Designer's Design Book
sourceRecords.notes: The primary origin of the four layout/design principles taught as C.R.A.P. — Contrast, Repetition, Alignment, Proximity — by Robin Williams. First edition 1994. Copyrighted; named and cited for attribution only, no text reproduced. The four-principle framework and the attribution are corroborated by the Saylor and Howdy-or-Hello OER sources.

sourceRecords.title: F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web: Misunderstood, But Still Relevant (Even on Mobile)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: the F-pattern was identified by NN/g via eye-tracking (2006) and confirmed in later studies; fixations concentrate at the top and left; it is a default tendency (not a law) that occurs with unformatted text and is broken by headings, bold text, images, and lists. Reused from source-registry; wording not reproduced.
